Building Safety Fund for addressing life safety fire risks associated with cladding in high rise buildings (England only): new applications from July 2022

New applications from 1 September 2025

From 1 September 2025, the Building Safety Fund will not accept new applications. Applications for government remediation funding for buildings over 11m in England are to be made to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS) and managed by Homes England. New applicants should visit the Building Remediation Hub to start their application. Further information on the CSS can be found in the Cladding Safety Scheme Overview.

The Building Safety Fund will continue to progress the funding and remediation of the buildings still in the Fund. The guidance below still applies to existing BSF applications.

Introduction

The government announced the Building Safety Fund (BSF or Fund) in the Budget on 11 March 2020, to fund the remediation of cladding on high-rise (18m or above with a 30cm tolerance) residential buildings.

The BSF will meet the cost of addressing life safety fire risks associated with cladding on high rise residential buildings where the Responsible Entity, (also referred to as the Applicant in this guidance) or agent acting on their behalf, are unwilling or unable to afford to do so. The Fund is part of the wider Building Safety Programme whose objectives are to ensure that residents of high-rise buildings are safe – and feel safe – in their homes now, and in the future.

The Fund was previously open for applications between June 2020 and July 2020. We want to ensure that those with buildings that are eligible but did not previously apply can now access funding.

The Fund reopened on 28 July 2022 for eligible buildings without a funding solution in place where a Fire Risk Appraisal of External Wall construction (FRAEW) following the methodology set out in PAS 9980:2022 can be provided which recommends that work to address life safety fire risks associated with cladding, or alternative mitigation work is required. The date of closure of the Fund to new applications will be published with reasonable notice.

From 1 September 2025, new applicants should visit the Building Remediation Hub to start their application. From 1 September 2025 all applications submitted through the Building Remediation Hub will be progressed through the Cladding Safety Scheme.

This guidance is for new applications to BSF made by the Responsible Entity. The Responsible Entity is the organisation that has the legal obligation or right to carry out the remediation works. The Responsible Entity may be the building’s freeholder or head leaseholder, registered provider of social housing or a management company or Right To Manage (RTM) company [footnote 1] that has primary responsibility for the repair of the property.

If you have already applied to the BSF during the June 2020 and July 2020 application process, please refer to the Eligibility section in this guidance which explains which rules apply to you.

From March 2024, some groups of buildings have been transferred from the Building Safety Fund (BSF) to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS) to progress through all the stages of funding. Applicants have been notified where this transfer impacts their buildings.

Fund overview

The BSF will cover reasonable eligible costs[footnote 2] for the works required to address the life safety fire risks associated with cladding on high-rise residential properties. If you applied to the BSF between 28 July 2022 and 9 May 2023, and your building(s) has been determined eligible, you can continue with that application. The guidance below continues to apply to your application.

Fund objectives

The objectives of the Building Safety Fund are that:

the historical life safety fire risks associated with cladding on high-rise residential buildings is addressed quickly and proportionately so that residents in those homes are safe.

leaseholder and resident communication and engagement on the project is effective;

projects are delivered on time and to budget; and

cost recovery from those responsible for the installation of cladding is maximised.

The Building Safety Act

The Building Safety Act received Royal Assent on 28 April 2022 and will come into force over the coming months. The Act includes measures to protect qualifying leaseholders from the costs of cladding remediation. It will also implement a number of policies aimed at improving the regulation of building safety in England.

We will continue to make funding available via the BSF for buildings which meet the eligibility criteria in this guidance, and other existing funding programmes. This includes funding for works that leaseholders would be obliged to pay for under their lease terms but who now qualify for protection from cladding remediation costs (as the holder of a qualifying lease[footnote 3] under Schedule 8 of the Building Safety Act.

Developer Pledge / Developer Remediation Contract

On 10 January 2022 the then Secretary of State for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities set out his approach to resetting building safety in England. This established the principle that leaseholders must be protected and that the industry responsible should pay to fix the problems it created.

On 13 April 2022, the department announced that leading residential developers had pledged to remediate life critical fire safety works in buildings over 11 metres that they have played a role in developing or refurbishing over the last 30 years in England. The Government wrote to developers on 30 January 2023 asking them to solidify their pledge and contractually commit to remediating unsafe buildings that they developed or refurbished. Developers who have signed the contract have also agreed to reimburse any funding received from government remediation programmes in relation to buildings they had a role in developing or refurbishing. Find the contract and details of the developers who have signed the contract.

The department will write to Applicants where the original developer of their building has signed the contract. This will include confirming where a developer has agreed to fund the remediation and/or mitigation works on this building, as recommended by an FRAEW following the methodology set out in PAS 9980:2022 and other industry standards relevant to ensuring the building meets a life critical safety standard. As a result of these commitments, the Department will not expect to award funding to buildings (applying after June 2022) covered by Developer contract commitment, unless otherwise agreed with the developer.

The Department will pursue those who played a role in developing unsafe buildings: it has taken powers through the Building Safety Act to hold industry to account; and has established a dedicated Recovery Unit that will identify and pursue companies that fail to do the right thing.

Proportionality and the introduction of PAS 9980:2022

A Publicly Available Specification (PAS) has been developed by the British Standards Institution named PAS 9980:2022. This contains recommendations and guidance tailored to the risks posed by fire spread over external walls; and provides tools for a competent professional to carry out a Fire Risk Appraisal of External Wall construction (FRAEW).

PAS 9980:2022 sets out steps that can be taken to identify and assess risk factors as well as mitigation steps that might improve the risk rating of a building via a holistic and fact-based assessment of a building’s construction.

For this reason, the Fund will use the recommendations and advice provided by external wall assessors in an FRAEW for its funding decisions. For new applications this will replace the requirements to demonstrate the presence of specific materials set out in technical guidance for existing Building Safety Fund applications.

Annex D of this guidance provides further information for Responsible Entities about how PAS9980:2022 will help support a risk based proportionate approach in new applications to the BSF.

As a consequence, to apply, buildings will be required to have an FRAEW following the methodology as set out by PAS 9980:2022 which recommends actions to address life safety fire risks associated with cladding. To note, buildings that started remediation (replacement and removal of cladding) work on or after 11 March 2020 but before 28 July 2022 should continue to follow the original BSF technical requirements on the removal and replacement of unsafe cladding systems.

New applicants commissioning FRAEWs from 8 April 2024 should have their FRAEW carried out by a panel member. You will receive details of the panel once you have completed the initial stage of your application. The use of a panel member is however not mandatory.

Scope of the fund

For private sector applicants, funding will be available for high-rise buildings (18m or above[footnote 4] with cladding where the Applicant can prove that it holds a qualifying legal interest in the building (being the correct Responsible Entity for MHCLG payment purposes and responsible for implementing appropriate and effective remediation solutions). It will also need to be proven from public records that there is at least one lease of a single unit of residential accommodation within the building that:

(a) was granted on market terms[footnote 5]; and

(b) requires the property to be used exclusively for residential occupation; and

(c) was granted on a date prior to 11 March 2020 at a premium and which was granted originally with a term (i.e. period) of not less than 21 years.

All the above criteria need to be met to be a Qualifying Lease.

For these buildings, BSF funding will be available for the full eligible costs of the project subject to the assessment of a full application.

In the social sector, Applicants can apply for the equivalent to the proportion of the Full Works and Costs (FWC) figure relating to any planned works that in the absence of the protections afforded by the Building Safety Act would otherwise be capable of allocation to residential leaseholders (whether market or shared ownership[footnote 6] or commercial leaseholders (operating businesses from commercial units in the building).[footnote 7]

Additionally, funding will be available to a Registered Provider of social housing or local authority[footnote 8] at a headline level in relation to the full cost of works where social sector landlords’ financial viability is threatened by the costs of works. The Department will only fund works where remediation costs threaten the financial viability of the provider or the Housing Revenue Account. For local authorities, this will require a declaration from a section 151 officer. Registered Providers (Housing Associations) will be required to provide a business case to the department setting out their financial position and options. The Regulator of Social Housing will be notified by MHCLG the intention to apply via this route. Unless specifically stated, this guidance is applicable to both social sector application routes.

In both the private and social sectors, funding for mixed use residential and commercial developments will be accepted. In both sectors, the fund will not be available for:

Buildings with cladding in scope where remediation works had been committed to, started on site, or had been completed prior to the Budget announcement on 11 March 2020.

other non-residential buildings, for example hotels, hospitals, offices and buildings where there are no residential leaseholders (unless applying from the social sector under the financial viability route).

purpose-built student accommodation, or where a lease specifies a property is to be used exclusively as student accommodation.

buildings developed as part of a Private Funding Initiative (PFI) scheme[footnote 9].

buildings under 18m in height (buildings 11-18 metres should apply to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS), delivered by Homes England.

buildings over 18m in height situated within London which are a part of a mixed height[footnote 10] development which includes other 11-18m buildings (these buildings should apply to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS), delivered by Homes England.

buildings 11m+ situated outside of London boroughs (as of 09 May 2023, these buildings should apply to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS), delivered by Homes England.

For residential buildings eligible for BSF, any unsafe ACM cladding[footnote 11] found will need to be removed and replaced, the costs of which will be eligible for government funding. Competent persons carrying out an FRAEW following the methodology set out in PAS9980:2022, should take this into account when undertaking the FRAEW.

Fund structure and administration

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) is the responsible department and the decision-making body for the fund.

MHCLG is working with the Greater London Authority (GLA) in London and Homes England outside London alongside MHCLG caseworkers to administer the fund as Delivery Partners. All Delivery Partners will draw on specialist expert legal and cost consultancy support to help assess applications.

In addition, we will make available expert specialist support for Applicants who need additional support to plan their works. You should discuss with your Delivery Partners if you believe you would benefit and want to be considered for this support. MHCLG strongly encourages, and may in specific circumstances require, Applicants to make use of this support from an early stage to help plan and deliver their project.

The following types of funding are available from the BSF:

Pre-Tender Support funding, where requested, which will only be made available once the application has been submitted and approved as eligible and you have signed the Short Form Funding Agreement for Pre-Tender Support.

Full Cost funding, which will only be made available once the application has been approved following an eligible assessment and you have signed the Grant Funding Agreement.

Your building being deemed eligible, or being approved for Pre-Tender Support, is not confirmation that you will get full funding. Applicants should therefore be aware that they may potentially be proceeding at risk until the point that the award of full funding has been confirmed by MHCLG and the GFA has been completed (i.e., dated) following execution.

Pre-Tender Support is not provided for social sector Applicants who are making an application for the share of costs which, in the absence of the Building Safety Act, would have been attributable to leaseholders. The department expects the Registered Provider to have the funds available to undertake pre-tender activities.

Driving the pace of remediation and enforcement

It is essential that life safety fire risks associated with cladding are addressed as quickly as possible to ensure that residents are safe and feel safe in their homes. Applications for the Fund must therefore be submitted without delay. We expect responsible entities to ensure they set out and follow a realistic, but ambitious project delivery timetable, and to keep Delivery Partners fully informed about any changes to those timetables.

The government supports local authorities and fire and rescue services in the use of their enforcement powers against buildings with fire risks associated with cladding. MHCLG regularly shares data from the Fund on the progress of applications with local authorities and fire and rescue services. Where projects are not progressing quickly enough, MHCLG will work with local authorities and fire and rescue services on their considerations of appropriate enforcement action.

Engaging with residents and leaseholders

Residents must be at the heart of building safety, with those responsible for remediation projects and works considering residents as a key stakeholder.

Throughout a remediation project, all residents and leaseholders should:

receive appropriate information and be meaningfully engaged;

be made aware of the likely impacts on their lives and understand how these impacts are being (and will be) identified, assessed, and managed; and

know what to expect from those responsible for delivering the project and where to go when they have questions or issues arise.

Our expectations

Building Safety Fund (BSF) applicants are expected to comply with the following:

Where there is any conflict between the Code of Considerate Practice and the Grant Funding Agreement (GFA), the provisions of the GFA prevail.

Keeping leaseholders and residents informed

In alignment with the Code of Practice for the Remediation of Residential Buildings, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) requires applicants (or their official managing agents) to provide regular, up-to-date communications about their BSF-funded remediation project to BSF building residents.

Notably, meaningful information should be provided at the following milestones and at any time upon request:

Diagram detailing different milestones in the BSF application process: 1) Initial application, 2) eligibility decision, 3) appeal information, 4) full application submission, 5) procurement of works, 6) full application approval and signing of funding agreement, 7) start of works, 8) remediation works completed.

The Building Safety Fund (BSF) Leaseholder and Resident Service is a secure online information portal that gives all residents in BSF buildings access to standard monthly updates on where their building is in the application process.

We email all applicants (and their nominated leaseholder where the applicant has named one in their initial application) a Unique Building Code, specific to each building in the BSF, along with details of the Service.

We expect applicants (or their official managing agent or nominated leaseholder where one has been assigned) to cascade this information to all BSF building residents so that they can use the Service. Applicants should not share this code with anyone else.

This Service is designed to encourage engagement. Importantly, it does not remove the need for regular resident communications/ engagement from applicants or their official managing agents.

Where regular updates are not provided and applicants/ managing agents are unreceptive to providing information, residents can and do report applicants to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) which we follow up.

For more information on what we expect from applicants, please read the requirements set out in Part 2 of the Code of Practice for the Remediation of Buildings, summarised below:

Diagram summarising the code of practice for engaging with residents and leaseholders: (1) regular communications meaningful engagement, setting out how and when residents will hear from you. (2) Understand the needs of residents. (3) Give residents opportunity to engage with decisions. (4) Residents should be able to meet those involved in delivering the project before it commences. (5) Communication methods must appropriately fits the needs of the residents. (6) Residents should be clear on how they can raise questions, issues and complaints.

Considering residents during remediation works

Applicants should ensure, or be assured, that any contractors or sub-contractors for their building’s remediation project:

consider the impact of works on residents, and

take reasonable steps to minimise these impacts on those occupying the building, thereby promoting a liveable environment.

This could include considering: the phasing of work, days/time of work, access to common spaces, maintaining ventilation and light, noise mitigation measures, measures to increase privacy, and site-security plans.

For more information on what we expect from applicants, please read the requirements set out in Part 3 of the Code of Practice for the Remediation of Buildings, summarised below:

Diagram summarising code of practice for engaging with residents during the project: (1) Include residents in design and delivery of the project. (2) Take reasonable steps to reduce impact of noise. (3) Take reasonable steps to avoid reducing light and ventilation. (4) Reduce impact of works requiring access to homes and common facilities in the building. (5) Ensure safety and security to building and residents. (6) Reduce disruption to residents required to leave homes temporarily during works.

Higher-risk buildings

In regulations, there are also additional requirements for higher-risk buildings. Higher-risk buildings are buildings with at least two residential units which are at least 18 metres or seven storeys high.

Every higher-risk occupied building must have at least one, named, accountable person. This person is responsible for the repair of the structure and exterior of the building.

For buildings with multiple accountable persons, there will be a principal accountable person. If there is only one accountable person, that person will be the principal accountable person.

As an accountable person for a higher-risk building, you have to:

keep residents informed about building safety,

provide certain information to all residents at specific points, including when new residents move into the building, and

provide additional information to residents on request.

As a principal accountable person for a higher-risk building you have to:

put in place a resident engagement strategy which ensures that residents have the opportunity to understand and participate in the safe management of their building,

put in place a complaints process for residents, covering complaints relevant to building safety, and

engage and work together with other accountable persons to ensure the resident engagement strategy and complaints process works effectively.

See guidance on developing a resident engagement strategy.

Additionally, the Building Safety Regulator has produced guidance for residents which can be found here: Residents of higher-risk buildings

Sources of information and support

We expect you to signpost residents to relevant information. This includes:

information on GOV.UK:

Finally, you should ensure that leaseholders are aware that they can get information and advice about their leases, rights or the BSF from the Leasehold Advisory Service (LEASE).

How to raise issues and make complaints

As mentioned:

under the Code of Practice for the Remediation of Residential Buildings, we expect all applicants (or their official managing agents) to outline to residents how they can raise issues and make complaints relating to your management of the BSF remediation project, and

under regulations, higher-risk buildings also must have a complaints process for building safety issues.

If residents are still dissatisfied with how you have handled their issue, they can complain directly to MHCLG

Any issues that you may have with MHCLG relating to the BSF, and which you have not been able to resolve with your BSF programme contacts, can also be raised through this complaints procedure.

Who can make an application for the Fund?

In the private sector, applications are open to the Responsible Entity (or an agent acting on their behalf) that has a building that meets the Eligibility criteria set out in the section below.

Further detail about buildings in scope can be found in Annex A: Technical guidance for applicants of BSF funding via the PAS 9980:2022.

In the social sector, applications are open to the Responsible Entity for a building, usually the Registered Provider of Social Housing (RP) that has a building that meets the Eligibility criteria set out in the section below.

Following receipt of your application the Fund’s appointed Legal Advisor will review your application to establish if the legal criteria for access to the Fund have been satisfied and as to whether you are entitled to be treated as the correct Responsible Entity. This being the case, we will be assured by our Delivery Partner that the legal eligibility tests have been met and you are an appropriate entity for MHCLG to enter into a grant funding agreement (or GFA) with.

Where multiple buildings have the same Responsible Entity, please complete one application for each building[footnote 12]. Where multiple buildings form a single development which is being covered by the same works contract, this should be mentioned in each of the individual applications.

Applications to the Fund should not be made, where there is no intention of drawing on taxpayer funding to complete the work.

Applications will not be accepted from leaseholders (unless they are the head leaseholder acting as the Responsible Entity), but they should encourage their landlords/building owners or managing agents for the building to register if costs of eligible works would otherwise be passed to leaseholders.

Applicants can appoint a representative to lead their application day-to-day and this may be a managing agent or the project manager.

Eligibility

The Fund is open to applications from responsible entities of private or social sector buildings that meet all of the following criteria:

buildings that are 18m or above

buildings which are within a London borough

buildings with at least one qualifying residential leaseholder (with exception of social sector landlords applying due to financial viability concerns),

the building must have cladding, as defined in the PAS9980:2022 (and set out in Annex A),

the building must have a Fire Risk Appraisal of External Wall construction (FRAEW) following the PAS 9980:2022 methodology which recommends actions to address life safety fire risks presented by the external wall system.

The BSF will not retrospectively fund work for buildings that committed to[footnote 13], started, or completed cladding removal and replacement work before 11 March 2020 when the Fund was first announced.

If you have a building that started the removal and replacement of cladding on or after 11 March 2020 (but before 28 July 2022), you will need to follow the Building Safety Fund for addressing life safety fire risks associated with cladding in high rise buildings (England only): Fund application guidance for buildings registered in 2020. You will need to provide a surveyor’s report such as an intrusive survey, facade or external wall report and “as built” drawings (which include the building height and the cladding materials) confirming the existence of cladding as set out in that guidance. If you do not have the above documents and materials have since been removed, you may also provide a signed statement from a surveyor stating that the materials were definitively on the building. You will not be required to provide an FRAEW.

If you have previously applied for the BSF (in June or July 2020), and your application was found to be eligible, you should continue with that application under the existing guidance.

If you previously applied to the BSF (in June or July 2020) and your application was found to be ineligible because the building was under 17.7m in height and did not meet the height criteria, apply to the Cladding Safety Scheme (CSS), delivered by Homes England.

If you previously applied to the BSF (in June or July 2020) and your application was found to be ineligible because the cladding was not eligible at the time, you can apply for the BSF if an FRAEW (as above) can be provided which meets the criteria set out in Annex A.

If you previously applied to the BSF (in June or July 2020) and your building was found to have ineligible works, or cladding systems that did not meet the specific criteria listed in Annex A – Technical Information of the 2020 BSF guidance, you may now be eligible for the BSF or CSS if an FRAEW following PAS 9980:2022 methodology can be provided which meets the criteria set out in Annex A.

The key objective of the Fund is to ensure that any life safety fire risks associated with cladding are addressed as quickly as possible to ensure that residents are safe and feel safe in their homes. Funding is available for residential or commercial leaseholders whether they benefit from protections against the requirement to pay service charges towards equivalent cladding remediation works (via commitments in their lease) - or not[footnote 14].

For buildings eligible for government funding, the Department expects any unsafe ACM cladding[footnote 15] found be removed and replaced, the costs of which will be eligible for government funding. This should be taken into account by the assessor when undertaking an FRAEW.

Providing additional support for buildings that need it

Additional support will be provided to buildings that have been identified as still using interim measures. Interim measures are urgent temporary measures which are to be put in place to address an ‘unacceptable risk to occupants’ of a building. These measures will vary depending on the risks associated with each individual building.

Buildings that are 11-18 metres in height

The Cladding Safety Scheme will provide funding for the management of unsafe cladding in England where a responsible developer cannot be identified, traced, or held responsible. It will be available to all eligible medium-rise buildings between 11-18 metres across England and applications for high-rise buildings over 18 metres outside of London. The scheme will be delivered by Homes England. If you need to apply for funding for a medium-rise building, visit the Cladding Safety Scheme page to start your application.

When and how to apply for funding

All Applicants should apply using the same application form, whether it is a private or social sector building. See the application form link and information on how to apply.

To apply for the Building Safety Fund, you will need an FRAEW following PAS 9980:2022 methodology and meet the eligibility criteria outlined above.

To obtain an FRAEW following PAS 9980:2022 methodology, you should appoint an appropriately qualified and competent professional with suitable experience of multi-storey residential buildings to carry this out.

Once you have received a finalised version of your FRAEW, you should ensure that it meets the expectation of the BSF, as set out in the Annex A: Technical guidance for applicants of BSF funding via the PAS 9980:2022. If you are content the FRAEW meets the standard required by the Fund, you should formally submit the FRAEW and apply to the BSF.

Guidance for Responsible Entities on getting an FRAEW and applying to the BSF can be found in Annex D. The process for quality assuring your FRAEW and supporting information is set out below.

The process for quality assuring your FRAEW and supporting information is set out below:

To assess eligibility for the Fund, Applicants will be required to complete the application form and submit an FRAEW carried out to PAS 9980:2022 methodology. Your application will then enter a 2 stage FRAEW Assurance process which involves a Triage Check followed by a Technical Check. You may be asked to revise and resubmit your FRAEW if it does not meet the requirements set out in Annex A. Once eligibility has been confirmed, the funded elements of your application will be reviewed, and then passed to Delivery Partners who will work with you to progress your application.

Once we have reviewed this information you will be informed in writing about the next stage of the application process.

Guidance for Applicants with FRAEWs that present multiple options for remediation

We expect the company that carried out your FRAEW to provide clear recommendations and justification for remedial action(s) (for more information see Annex A of the Building Safety Fund Guidance).

If your FRAEW has identified multiple options, following our review of your FRAEW we will provide you with a certificate for completion.

This will require you to consider the criteria in the box below when specifying your chosen remediation option(s) for your building wall types.

You will need to apply the criteria below when deciding which remediation option to pursue for each wall type(s).

Criteria:

It is expected that you:

Consider value for money and choose a solution where the costs of the remedial works pursued are reasonable and are proportionate to the level of risk present.

Ensure your project team are considerate to the needs of residents and leaseholders when considering the remediation options, recognising that any planned works are likely to be disruptive and this impact should be mitigated where possible. The Code of Practice for the Remediation of Residential Buildings sets out the Government’s expectations on how this should be done (for further details see ‘keeping leaseholders and residents informed’).

Engage the original FRAEW assessor and/or appropriate professional to ensure that the proposed works to address fire risks to life safety presented by the external wall system will reduce risks to a tolerable level.

You may need additional consultants to help you decide which option to pursue and your original FRAEW assessor should be able to assist with which professionals you may need to appoint.

Establishing works specification

Following confirmation that we will fund works to address life safety fire risks identified within your FRAEW, you will need to establish a works specification, working closely with your Delivery Partner to complete the application process. It is imperative that you do this at pace, keeping your Delivery Partner advised at all stages particularly if there are any changes or issues arising.

Significant work will be needed to get you to a point where you can go out to tender your project, including scoping the project, appointing a professional team, and developing a works specification. You must not appoint any party who was involved with the original works which are now being addressed by the BSF, without notifying your delivery partner first and ensuring you meet the conditions relating to procurement specified later in this guidance.

As part of the assessment of your application, we will estimate the total eligible costs for each building benchmarked against industry cost data. We will use this to check the reasonableness of your costs as part of our assessment process throughout your project’s lifecycle.

If you are eligible, you can apply for ‘pre-tender support’ if you need funding to get to this stage. Pre-tender support will only be provided following confirmation that we will fund the works to address the life safety fire risks identified within your FRAEW passed the initial legal due diligence and the project cannot progress without this support. Pre-tender support will usually be limited to 10% of the estimated cost of work.

If you do not proceed with the works or your full application turns out to be ineligible, we reserve the right to recoup the value of this initial pre-tender funding from you. Where pre-tender support has been spent to help to progress a project, but an eligible full costs application is not subsequently received, we will only seek to recoup this funding in the special circumstances set out in the Short Form Funding Agreement.

You can only submit a full costs application once you have gone out to tender and have a preferred contractor to carry out the works. At that point, you will be able to provide the required cost breakdown and answer the full works and costs related questions.

If costs are above the defined threshold of the benchmark, we will need to explore this further with you. We expect costs to be reasonable and comparative within the market, including fees. It remains your responsibility to produce the required information accurately, and as quickly as you can so we can progress your application.

Further checks

The full application process will involve legal, and project related, due diligence to ensure MHCLG is paying the correct Responsible Entity. This will allow it to implement appropriate and effective solutions, so that payment is only made where applications meet all the relevant eligibility criteria, and where a grant funding agreement in terms acceptable to MHCLG has been completed.

You will need to answer questions about your suitability to receive funding as the Responsible Entity for the Building (based on the legal eligibility criteria for access to the Fund set out in this guidance) and the ownership structure of the Building. Our Delivery Partners and their legal advisors will assess the provisions of a nominated lease document to ensure that there is a Qualifying Lease present in the records for the Building held at Land Registry and to confirm that the legal eligibility requirements have been satisfied.

You will also need to answer questions about the building itself. We will carry out due diligence on the information you provide before providing any funding for pre-tender support or full support for the works and reserve the right to reject an application in the event that it fails to meet the criteria set out in this guidance.

In summary key factors we will assess during this stage of the application process are:

whether Applicant details match publicly held records,

whether the Applicant is either required (via obligations owed to the leaseholders) to conduct any planned remediation works (whether or not these are chargeable to leaseholders) or entitled to do so either via its ownership of the building or rights provided to it by the lease documents (for example in the case of a named manager in the leases),

whether there is a Qualifying Lease present in the building’s online records at Land Registry,

confirmation of appointment of your Competent Professionals[footnote 16],

whether your costs for eligible works are reasonable,

when you will start on site or execute the ‘Works contract’[footnote 17],

how you will monitor progress and evaluate costs,

obtaining all statutory approvals including planning permissions,

your forecast start, and practical completion dates,

the reasonable efforts you have made to recover costs.

MHCLG will make decisions on the approval of applications. Where an application has not yet been developed to the stage at which construction can commence, early funding (pre-tender support) may be available for this design subject to a satisfactory application.

What we will fund

Where an FRAEW following PAS 9980:2022 methodology has recommended action to address life safety fire risks associated with cladding, we will fund reasonable capital costs [footnote 18] associated with these works on high-rise residential buildings.

We cover a wide range of direct project costs relating to the reduction of life safety fire risks associated with cladding, including:

Cost recovery

As set out above, a number of major residential developers have signed a contract committing them to remediate life critical fire safety works in buildings over 11 metres that they have played a role in developing or refurbishing over the last 30 years in England. Developers making this commitment have also agreed to reimburse any funding received from government remediation programmes in relation to buildings they had a role in developing or refurbishing.

Where the developer who built or refurbished the building subject to the application is not funding the fire safety works, and where the Responsible Entity is unable to do so, then the BSF will cover all reasonable eligible costs to address the life safety fire risks associated with cladding. Find out more information about the Developer Contract.

However, you are required to demonstrate that you have taken all reasonable steps to recover the costs of addressing the life safety fire risks associated with the cladding from those responsible through insurance claims, warranties, legal action etc. During the application process we will ask for information regarding such steps and may seek further information to satisfy ourselves of the position.

You may be able to recover costs from those responsible for historical defects on your building if construction was complete on or after 28 June 1992. This is because the Building Safety Act has extended the limitation period of the Defective Premises Act 1972 (DPA) to 30 years. Further information is in section 135 of the Act and its associated Explanatory Notes. If work was completed at any time in the 12 months after 28 June 1992, you have until 27 June 2023 to initiate proceedings, otherwise, the 30-year limitation will apply.

Where you do successfully recover damages relating to eligible works, Responsible Entities are required to pay the government any amounts recovered. The payments to government may be less any unrecovered legal fees that have been incurred when cost recovery efforts are successful.

We will not seek to recoup amounts recovered in litigation or settlement which do not relate to eligible works. Where Responsible Entities have already recovered damages, they should deduct relevant amounts in their applications and provide an explanation as to how this has been calculated. You can show these deductions as part of the ‘other requirements’ entries in the full works and costs spreadsheet.

MHCLG does not rule out seeking an assignment of relevant rights of action where it considers it would be appropriate to do so.

In circumstances where third parties such as competent professionals or chosen contractors do not perform their contractual obligations as part of their agreements reached with the Responsible Entity and, as a result, fund monies are not properly applied, MHCLG requires the Responsible Entity to take all steps necessary to recover any such fund monies. Building work carried out on a building must meet the requirements of the Building Regulations, including minimum standards for fire safety and energy efficiency.

Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII)

Your main contractor and all members of the Design Team must have PII with a minimum limit of £1 million or of no less than the total cost of the works (whichever is higher), capped at £10 million. This means that if the cost of works is greater than £10 million, only a maximum of £10 million of cover will be required. This must be maintained for 6 years if available at commercially reasonable rates and terms. The insurance must not have any exclusions for fire safety or cladding-related projects.

Your Design Team are any contractors or consultants which hold Material Design Responsibility. Material Design Responsibility means responsibility for any design which is integral to the structure or the fabric (including, without limitation, roofing, cladding or any other waterproofing) of the building.

In September 2022, the department agreed a new model insurance clause with the International Underwriting Association (IUA) covering fire safety risks in order to increase the availability of PII without exclusions. This is freely available for insurers to use for cladding remediation work on high-rise residential buildings which is funded by the BSF.

As part of this agreement with the IUA, the measures which are required by the clause are compulsory for all BSF projects. As a summary, what this means for Applicants is that their project must:

1) Have a clerk of works, who is independent of the Design Team, appointed on the project to oversee all works. This can be a chartered member of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) or the Chartered Institute of Building (CIOB) or a member of the Institute of Clerk of Works and Construction Inspectorate (ICWCI) or the Society of Façade Engineering (SFE) with experience of fire safety in high-rise residential buildings.

2) Have a competent professional (as defined by the clause), who is independent of the Design Team, to perform to inspect works at key milestones of the project to confirm compliance with the original design of the works. This is an adaptation of existing risk mitigations for projects with insufficient PII. These milestones are:

When 20% of funding is expended.

When 40% of funding is expended.

When 60% of funding is expended

When 80% of funding is expended.

At the point of Practical Completion.

These milestones should be informed by your Cost Consultant. The party performing the inspections will be required to complete a Compliance Report at each milestone. Template wording for these reports can be found in the GFA.

3) Ensure the required project management measures are followed.

You can find the full details of these requirements and the insurance clause.

These requirements will not apply if you have already received full funding approval before 18 November. However, where your main contractor and/or Design Team does not meet the PII requirements for the BSF, you should ask them to explore with insurers whether they are able to access this clause at the point of their next renewal if these new requirements are followed.

Should you still be unable to appoint a main contractor and Design Team with sufficient PII, or should they be unable to access this clause from insurers, you should consider whether the following solutions are viable:

Paying additional money to buy out any policy exclusion. Reasonable increases in the costs of appointing consultants or contractors in order to buy out policy exclusions or increase cover will be eligible for funding.

Sub-contracting design/fire safety liability to a consultant with sufficient PII.

This is in addition to still following the above requirements.
